paragraphs: “Oh, stop it! That’s all stupid, I don’t want to listen. I thought it would be fun,” Grushenka snapped at them suddenly.

Mitya flinched and stopped laughing at once. The tall Pole stood up. He looked bored and out of place, and with a haughty air he began pacing from corner to corner of the room, hands clasped behind his back.
“Ah, he can’t sit still,” said Grushenka, eyeing him with scorn. Mitya began to feel uneasy. He also noticed that the Pole on the sofa kept looking at him with irritation.
“_Panie!_” cried Mitya. “Come, let’s drink! You and the other _pan_, too! Let’s all drink.”
In a flash he had dragged three glasses over and filled them with champagne.
“To Poland, _panovie_! I drink to your Poland!” cried Mitya.
“With great pleasure, _panie_,” said the Pole on the sofa, with dignity and a friendly, lordly air, and he picked up his glass.
“And the other _pan_, what’s his name? Drink, most illustrious, take your glass!” Mitya urged.
“Pan Vrublevsky,” put in the Pole on the sofa.
Pan Vrublevsky came over to the table, rolling a little as he walked.
“To Poland, _panovie!_” cried Mitya, lifting his glass. “Hurrah!”
All three drank. Mitya grabbed the bottle and filled three glasses again.
“Now to Russia, _panovie_, and let’s be brothers!”
“Pour some for us,” said Grushenka. “I’ll drink to Russia, too!”
“So will I,” said Kalganov.
“And I will, too ... to Russia, the old grandmother!” tittered Maximov.
“Everybody! Everybody!” cried Mitya. “Trifon Borissovitch, bring more bottles!”
The other three bottles Mitya had brought with him were set on the table. Mitya filled the glasses.
“To Russia! Hurrah!” he shouted again. Everyone drank the toast except the Poles, and Grushenka downed her whole glass in one go. The Poles left theirs untouched.
“What’s this, _panovie_?” cried Mitya. “Won’t you drink?”
Pan Vrublevsky took his glass, raised it and said in a ringing voice:
“To Russia as she was before 1772.”
“Now that’s more like it!” cried the other Pole, and they both emptied their glasses at once.
“You’re fools, you _panovie_,” Mitya blurted out suddenly.
“_Panie!_” shouted both Poles in a threatening way, bristling at Mitya like a pair of fighting cocks. Pan Vrublevsky was the angrier of the two.
“Can a man help loving his own country?” he shouted.

“Quiet! No quarreling! I won’t have it!” cried Grushenka in a commanding voice, and she stamped her foot on the floor. Her face was flushed and her eyes were bright. The glass she had just drunk was clearly working on her. Mitya was badly frightened.
“_Panovie_, forgive me! It was my fault, I’m sorry. Vrublevsky, _panie_ Vrublevsky, I’m sorry.”
“You, anyway, shut your mouth! Sit down, you idiot!” Grushenka scolded, angry and annoyed.
They all sat down. Nobody spoke; they just looked at one another.
“Gentlemen, it was all my fault,” Mitya began again, unable to make sense of Grushenka’s words. “Well, why are we just sitting here? What can we do ... to have some fun again?”
“Ach, nothing here is fun at all!” Kalganov mumbled lazily.
“Let’s play faro again, like we did a while ago,” Maximov tittered suddenly.
“Faro? Splendid!” cried Mitya. “If only the _panovie_—”
“It’s lite, _panovie_,” the Pole on the sofa answered, as though reluctantly.
“True,” agreed Pan Vrublevsky.
“Lite? What’s that, ‘lite’?” asked Grushenka.
“Late, _pani_! I mean ‘a late hour,’” the Pole on the sofa explained.

“With them it’s always late. They can never do anything!” Grushenka almost shrieked in her anger. “They’re dull themselves, so they want everyone else dull, too. Before you came, Mitya, they sat here just as silent and kept turning up their noses at me.”
“My goddess!” cried the Pole on the sofa. “I see you’re not kindly toward me, and that is why I’m gloomy. I’m ready, _panie_,” he added, turning to Mitya.
“Go ahead, _panie_,” Mitya agreed. He pulled his notes out of his pocket and put two hundred-rouble notes on the table. “I want to lose a lot to you. Take your cards. Deal the bank.”
“We’ll take the cards from the landlord, _panie_,” said the little Pole, gravely and firmly.
“That’s much the best way,” chimed in Pan Vrublevsky.
“From the landlord? Fine, I see, we’ll get them from him. Cards!” Mitya shouted to the landlord.

The landlord brought a new pack, still sealed. He told Mitya that the girls were getting ready and the Jews with the cymbals would probably arrive soon, but the cart with the provisions had not come yet. Mitya jumped up from the table and ran into the next room to give instructions. Only three girls had turned up, though, and Marya wasn’t there yet. And he himself didn’t know what instructions to give, or why he had run out. All he did was tell them to unpack the presents for the girls from the box, the sweets, the toffee and the fondants. “And vodka for Andrey, vodka for Andrey!” he cried in a hurry. “I was rude to Andrey!”
Suddenly Maximov, who had followed him out, tapped him on the shoulder.
“Give me five roubles,” he whispered to Mitya. “I’ll put something on faro, too, he he!”
“Capital! Splendid! Take ten, here!”
Again he pulled all the notes out of his pocket and picked out a ten-rouble one. “And if you lose that, come back, come back.”

“Very good,” Maximov whispered joyfully, and scurried back. Mitya went back too, apologizing for keeping them waiting. The Poles had sat down and opened the pack. They looked far friendlier now, almost warm. The Pole on the sofa had lit another pipe and was getting ready to deal. He had a solemn look about him.
“Take your places, gentlemen,” cried Pan Vrublevsky.
“No, I won’t play any more,” said Kalganov. “I just lost fifty roubles to them.”
“The _pan_ had no luck. Maybe he’ll be lucky this time,” the Pole on the sofa said, turning to him.
“How much is in the bank? Enough to match me?” asked Mitya.
“It depends, _panie_. A hundred, maybe two hundred, as much as you care to stake.”
“A million!” laughed Mitya.
“Perhaps the Pan Captain has heard of Pan Podvysotsky?”
“What Podvysotsky?”

“In Warsaw there was a bank, and anyone at all could come and bet against it. Podvysotsky comes, sees a thousand gold pieces, bets against the bank. The banker says, ‘_Panie_ Podvysotsky, are you putting down the gold, or are we to trust your honor?’ ‘My honor, _panie_,’ says Podvysotsky. ‘So much the better.’ The banker throws the dice. Podvysotsky wins. ‘Take it, _panie_,’ says the banker, and he pulls out the drawer and gives him a million. ‘Take it, _panie_, this is what you won.’ There was a million in the bank. ‘I didn’t know that,’ says Podvysotsky. ‘_Panie_ Podvysotsky,’ said the banker, ‘you pledged your honor and we pledged ours.’ Podvysotsky took the million.”
“That’s not true,” said Kalganov.
“_Panie_ Kalganov, in gentlemen’s company one does not say such things.”

“As if a Polish gambler would hand over a million!” cried Mitya, but he checked himself at once. “Forgive me, _panie_, my fault again. He would, he would hand over a million, for honor, for Polish honor. See how well I speak Polish, ha ha! Here, I bet ten roubles, the knave leads.”

“And I put one rouble on the queen, the queen of hearts, the pretty little _panienotchka_, he he!” laughed Maximov. He drew out his queen and, as though trying to hide it from everybody, edged right up close and crossed himself quickly under the table. Mitya won. The rouble won, too.
“A corner!” cried Mitya.
“I’ll bet one more rouble, a ‘single’ stake,” Maximov muttered gleefully, enormously pleased at having won a rouble.
“Lost!” shouted Mitya. “A ‘double’ on the seven!”
The seven was beaten as well.
“Stop!” cried Kalganov suddenly.
“Double! Double!” Mitya doubled his stakes, and every time he doubled a card, the Poles beat it. The rouble stakes kept winning.
“Double again!” shouted Mitya furiously.
“You have lost two hundred, _panie_. Will you stake another hundred?” the Pole on the sofa asked.
“What? Two hundred gone already? Then two hundred more! All doubles!”
And pulling the money from his pocket, Mitya was about to throw two hundred roubles down on the queen, but Kalganov covered it with his hand.
“Enough!” he shouted in his ringing voice.
“What’s the matter with you?” Mitya stared at him.
“Enough! I don’t want you playing any more. Don’t!”
“Why?”
“Because I don’t want it. Blast it, come away. That’s why. I won’t let you keep playing.”
Mitya looked at him in amazement.
“Give it up, Mitya. Maybe he’s right. You’ve lost plenty already,” said Grushenka, with a curious note in her voice. Both Poles stood up, looking deeply offended.
“Are you joking, _panie_?” said the short man, giving Kalganov a stern look.
“How dare you!” Pan Vrublevsky growled at Kalganov, too.
“Don’t you dare shout like that,” cried Grushenka. “Ah, you turkey-cocks!”
Mitya looked from one to the other. But something in Grushenka’s face suddenly caught his attention, and in that same instant a new idea flashed into his head—a strange new idea!
“_Pani_ Agrippina,” the little Pole was starting, red with anger, when Mitya suddenly stepped up to him and clapped him on the shoulder.
“Most illustrious, a word with you.”
“What do you want?”
“In the next room. I have two words to tell you, something pleasant, very pleasant. You’ll be glad to hear it.”
The little _pan_ was startled and gave Mitya a wary look. Still, he agreed straight away, on condition that Pan Vrublevsky went with them.
“The bodyguard? Let him come, I want him, too. I must have him!” cried Mitya. “March, _panovie_!”
“Where are you going?” asked Grushenka, anxious.
“We’ll be back in a moment,” Mitya answered.
There was a kind of daring in his eyes, a sudden confidence. His face had looked very different when he came into the room an hour before.

He led the Poles not to the big room where the chorus of girls was gathering and the table was being laid, but to the bedroom on the right. The trunks and packages were kept there, and there were two large beds, each with a heap of cotton pillows piled up like a pyramid. A candle was burning on a small deal table in the corner. The little man and Mitya sat down at this table across from each other, while the huge Vrublevsky stood by them with his hands behind his back. The Poles looked stern but plainly wanted to know what was coming.
“What can I do for you, _panie_?” lisped the little Pole.
“Well, look here, _panie_, I won’t keep you long. Here’s money for you,” and he took out his notes. “Do you want three thousand? Take it and be on your way.”
The Pole stared at Mitya, wide-eyed, with a probing look.
“Three thousand, _panie_?” He exchanged a glance with Vrublevsky.

“Three, _panovie_, three! Listen, _panie_, I can see you’re a sensible man. Take the three thousand and go to the devil, and take Vrublevsky with you—do you hear? But at once, this very minute, and for good. You understand, _panie_, for good. There’s the door, go out through it. What have you got there, a greatcoat, a fur coat? I’ll bring it out to you. They’ll bring the horses round straight away, and then—good-by, _panie_!”
Mitya waited for an answer, sure of himself. He had no doubts at all. A look of extraordinary determination came over the Pole’s face.
“And the money, _panie_?”

“The money, _panie_? Five hundred roubles I’ll give you this very moment for the journey, as a first payment, and two thousand five hundred tomorrow in town—I swear on my honor, I’ll get it, I’ll get it at any price!” cried Mitya.
The Poles exchanged glances again. The short man’s face grew more forbidding.

“Seven hundred, seven hundred, not five hundred, right now, this minute, cash in hand!” Mitya added, sensing that something was wrong. “What’s the matter, _panie_? Don’t you trust me? I can’t hand over the whole three thousand all at once. If I did, you might come back to her tomorrow.... Besides, I haven’t got the three thousand on me. It’s at home in town,” faltered Mitya, his heart sinking with every word. “On my word, the money is there, hidden away.”
In an instant a remarkable sense of his own dignity appeared on the little man’s face.
“What next?” he asked sarcastically. “For shame!” and he spat on the floor. Pan Vrublevsky spat too.
“You’re doing that, _panie_,” said Mitya, seeing with despair that it was all over, “because you hope to get more out of Grushenka? You’re a pair of capons, that’s what you are!”

“This is a mortal insult!” The little Pole went red as a crab and walked out of the room briskly, as if he couldn’t bear to hear another word. Vrublevsky lumbered out after him, and Mitya followed, confused and crushed. He was afraid of Grushenka, afraid the _pan_ would start shouting right away. And so he did. The Pole came into the room and flung himself down before Grushenka in a theatrical pose.
“_Pani_ Agrippina, I have suffered a mortal insult!” he exclaimed. But Grushenka suddenly lost all patience, as though they had hurt her in her most tender spot.
“Speak Russian! Speak Russian!” she cried. “Not another word of Polish! You used to speak Russian. You can’t have forgotten it in five years.”
She was red with fury.
“_Pani_ Agrippina—”
“My name is Agrafena, Grushenka. Speak Russian or I won’t listen!”
The Pole gasped with offended dignity and quickly and pompously said in broken Russian:
“_Pani_ Agrafena, I came here to forget the past and forgive it, to forget all that happened up to today—”
“Forgive? You came here to forgive me?” Grushenka cut him off, leaping up from her seat.

“Exactly so, _pani_. I am not pusillanimous, I am magnanimous. But I was astounded when I saw your lovers. Pan Mitya offered me three thousand, in the other room, to go away. I spat in the _pan’s_ face.”
“What? He offered you money for me?” cried Grushenka, hysterical. “Is that true, Mitya? How dare you? Am I for sale?”
“_Panie, panie!_” yelled Mitya. “She’s pure and shining, and I have never been her lover! That’s a lie....”

“How dare you stand up for me to him?” shrieked Grushenka. “It wasn’t virtue that kept me pure, and it wasn’t fear of Kuzma. I did it so I could hold my head up when I met him, and call him a scoundrel to his face. And did he really turn down the money?”
“He took it! He took it!” cried Mitya. “Only he wanted all three thousand at once, and I could give him just seven hundred on the spot.”
“I see: he heard I had money, and came here to marry me!”
“_Pani_ Agrippina!” cried the little Pole. “I am—a knight, I am—a nobleman, and not a _lajdak_. I came here to make you my wife, and I find you a different woman, perverse and shameless.”

“Oh, go back where you came from! I’ll tell them to throw you out, and out you’ll go,” cried Grushenka, furious. “What a fool I’ve been, a fool, to be so miserable these five years! And it wasn’t even for his sake, it was my own anger that made me miserable. And this isn’t he at all! Was he like this? This could be his father! Where did you get that wig? He was a falcon, and this is a gander. He used to laugh and sing for me.... And I’ve been crying for five years, damned fool that I was, wretched and shameless!”
She sank back into her low chair and hid her face in her hands. At that moment the Mokroe chorus began to sing in the room on the left—a rollicking dance song.
“A regular Sodom!” Vrublevsky roared suddenly. “Landlord, drive those shameless hussies out!”
The landlord had been peering curiously in at the door for some time. Now he heard the shouting and guessed that his guests were quarreling, and he came into the room at once.
“What are you yelling for? Do you want to burst your throat?” he said to Vrublevsky, with astonishing rudeness.
“Animal!” bellowed Pan Vrublevsky.

“Animal? And what kind of cards were you playing with just now? I gave you a pack and you hid it. You played with marked cards! I could send you to Siberia for playing with false cards, do you know that? It’s the same as forging banknotes....”
And going over to the sofa, he stuck his fingers between the back and the cushion and pulled out a sealed pack of cards.
“Here’s my pack, still sealed!”
He held it up and showed it to everyone in the room. “From where I stood I saw him slip my pack away and put his own in its place—you’re a cheat and no gentleman!”
“And I saw the _pan_ switch a card twice!” cried Kalganov.
“How shameful! How shameful!” exclaimed Grushenka, wringing her hands and blushing with real shame. “Good Lord, he’s sunk to this!”
“I thought so, too!” said Mitya. But before he had finished saying it, Vrublevsky, his face confused and furious, shook his fist at Grushenka and shouted:
“You low harlot!”
Mitya was on him at once. He seized him with both hands, lifted him off the floor, and in a moment had carried him into the room on the right, the one they had just left.
“I’ve put him down on the floor in there,” he announced, coming straight back, panting with excitement. “He’s struggling, the scoundrel! But he won’t come back, never fear!...”
He shut one half of the folding doors and, holding the other half open a crack, called out to the little Pole:
“Most illustrious, would you care to go out as well?”
“My dear Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” said Trifon Borissovitch, “make them give back the money you lost. It’s as good as stolen from you.”
“I don’t want my fifty roubles back,” Kalganov declared suddenly.
“And I don’t want my two hundred, either,” cried Mitya. “I wouldn’t take it for anything! Let him keep it as a consolation.”
“Bravo, Mitya! You’re a prince, Mitya!” cried Grushenka, and there was a note of fierce anger in her cry.
The little _pan_, red with fury but still careful of his dignity, was heading for the door. He stopped short, though, and said suddenly to Grushenka:
“_Pani_, if you want to come with me, come. If not, good-by.”

And swollen with indignation and self-importance, he went to the door. He was a man of character: he thought so highly of himself that even after all that had happened he still expected her to marry him. Mitya slammed the door behind him.
“Lock it,” said Kalganov. But the key clicked on the other side; they had locked it from inside.
“That’s perfect!” exclaimed Grushenka without mercy. “It serves them right!”
